findings.title: The new version's Linux x64 engine does not build the way the release builds it
findings.what: The release workflow (package.yml, and release-cache.yml on main and nightly) links the Linux engine with napi-rs's cross toolchain (glibc 2.17, GCC 4.8.5, libstdc++ 6.0.19) so it loads on old distributions; 0.1.5 builds that way in 241.7 s on the same machine (4 jobs), its engine needing nothing past glibc 2.17. At the new version the link of the new rerail-engine command-line binary fails after 705 s, on two causes and one more symbol. (1) gettid, which glibc exports from 2.30, is called in native/src/code_rule_dsl/logic/profile.rs:1125, native/src/threads.rs:34 and native/src/test_watchdog.rs:40; libc::syscall(libc::SYS_gettid) gives the same id on every glibc. Even if it linked, the engine would need glibc 2.30, above the 2.28 floor docs/installation.md states. (2) The simdjson shim (simdjson 5.0.5, C++17): the cross toolchain's g++ 4.8.5 has no -std=c++17, and cc ignores the TARGET_CXX napi sets when host and target match, so the host's g++ compiles it and the link misses sized operator delete and std::__cxx11::basic_string members (13 references). SQLite's C code, compiled the same way, adds a reference to fcntl64 (glibc 2.28). 0.1.5's published engine holds the same fcntl64 reference: a shared library may leave it to load time, an executable must resolve it at the link. A probe of the shim alone: with the old string ABI and -fno-sized-deallocation, 6 references to __libc_single_threaded (glibc 2.32) remain. No compiler flag alone fixes it; the choices are to build the Linux engine on a newer floor (a glibc 2.28 toolchain with a C++17 compiler, Node 24's own floor), to leave the simdjson part out of the old-glibc build as MSVC builds already do, or to link a newer libstdc++ statically against the sysroot's headers (not tried). The pull request's checks and CI's build job use the host's toolchain (npm run build:native), so none shows it; the first release after the merge, and the nightly release cache on main, would fail.

findings.title: The new version does not merge cleanly with 0.1.5
findings.what: Merging 0.1.5 into the new version conflicts in src/engine/catalog/rule-packs.ts, docs/rule-packs.md and docs/privacy.md: 0.1.5 leaves out a pack made for a newer Rerail (#715), and the new version changes how the same loader treats a pack whose token rules it refuses. The branch needs main merged again, with these three files resolved by hand, before it can land on 0.1.5.

findings.title: Six of our nine fixes merge into the new version as they are; two conflict in a few lines, and #677 brings 0.1.5's three
findings.what: fix 2, fix 4, fix 5 (#674), fix 6, #665 and #676 merge clean; #677's own changes merge clean, but its branch brings 0.1.5's last commits and their conflicts in docs/privacy.md, docs/rule-packs.md and src/engine/catalog/rule-packs.ts. With each fix merged, its test files pass at the new version (1,027 tests in all, 0 failed, Linux). With the fix taken out and its tests kept, they fail at the new version (fix 2: 19 tests, fix 5: 126, fix 6: 22, #665: 9, #676: 3, #677: 1; fix 4's 6 new test files cannot load), so the new version has every defect these fixes remove. fix 1 conflicts in ci.yml, native/src/lib.rs and native.ts (4 hunks, 23 lines), fix 3 in one import line of a test; main + six fixes as a whole conflicts in exactly those four files (5 hunks, 25 lines).

findings.title: A build with nothing changed recompiles the whole engine crate, at 0.1.5 and at the new version
findings.what: Running npm run build:native (or the release command) a second time with no change rebuilds the rerail-engine crate: 162 s at 0.1.5 on Linux (4 jobs), 456 s at the new version on Windows (8 virtual CPUs), about the cost of a one-line edit. Something the engine's build script watches changes on every build. A contributor pays it on every build; it is not new in the new version, but the new version's larger engine crate makes it longer.

findings.title: On Windows, the engine library and the new rerail-engine binary write the same PDB file
findings.what: the new version's Windows build warns twice: 'output filename collision at ...\\release\\rerail_engine.pdb' (and in deps/): the cdylib and the CLI binary of the same name both write rerail_engine.pdb, so one overwrites the other's debug symbols. Cargo says this may become a hard error. Renaming the binary's target or its PDB removes it.

findings.title: On Linux no test fails at the new version that passes at 0.1.5
findings.what: Same host, same commands, one after the other: unit tests 8,711 passed, 46 failed at the new version against 8,652 passed, 49 failed at 0.1.5, every failure at the new version also failing at 0.1.5 (they need the pack test data no test host has); integration 90 passed at both. The 8,580 unit tests that pass at both took 1,099.6 s at the new version against 1,063.2 s (+3.4%). Rust tests: the new version 4,236 passed and 11 failed against 1,588 and 3 at 0.1.5; 10 of the new version's failures read the missing pack test data, and the eleventh (git_ignore ... the index is re-read once it changes) failed once in the full run and passed 20 of 20 alone at the new version, as at 0.1.5: a test that depends on timing under load.

findings.title: An upgrade starts every repository from an empty content store
findings.what: The new version opens content-v4.sqlite where 0.1.5 opens content-v1.sqlite, so the first checks after the upgrade derive every repository's content again; the old file and its -wal and -shm stay on disk until the person deletes them.

findings.title: 40 of the 942 rules in the 12 published packs do not run at the new version until their packs are republished
findings.what: Compiled one by one as the catalog does before it loads a pack: at the new version, 15 javascript, 16 python, 8 typescript and 1 php rule are refused as testing a token the new version's syntax trees leave out; each pack still loads and the rule is reported as skipped. At 0.1.5 all 942 compile.

findings.title: npm run check fails at the new version
findings.what: check:structure refuses the rule documents under docs/rule-syntax/ and gate/data-layer/ (outside packs/<id>/rules/ and fixtures/), as the pull request's known red checks say; at 0.1.5 the same command passes.

findings.title: The new version builds on Windows 11 and its engine needs no Visual C++ runtime
findings.what: A real MSVC build (not only a type-check): 1,221 s cold on 8 virtual CPUs against 420 s for 0.1.5; the engine is 122.3 MB against 42.3 MB and passes the release's check-windows-runtime.mjs. MSVC leaves simdjson's native part out, so Windows reads JSON without it.
